nodes.label: M0 — Stabilise
nodes.rationale: The build failed with 18 TypeScript errors, the schema and every RLS policy existed only inside the hosted Supabase project, and strict was off in all three tsconfigs. Nothing else in the plan can proceed safely until the project compiles, its security boundary is reviewable in Git, and a second environment can be created.

nodes.label: M1 — Foundation
nodes.rationale: Six structural defects (per-call-site auth subscriptions, global query keys, no error surface, a drop path with no rollback) are all touched by the ownership migration anyway — fixing them before M2 costs days, after M2 it costs weeks.

nodes.label: M2 — Boards
nodes.rationale: Every remaining MVP feature is structurally impossible against a user_id foreign key, because there is no query that can share a board when there is no board. The milestone the whole architecture review existed for; XL, 21 tasks, destructive data migration across every table.

nodes.label: M3 — Members & Roles
nodes.rationale: Boards without members are just namespaced personal boards. Before M3 'can I edit this?' was answered by 'do you own the board'; afterwards it is a role lookup that must happen in the database, not in React. Closed 2026-08-14 with 209 verification cases green on a replica.

nodes.label: M4 — Invitations
nodes.rationale: M3 makes membership mutable by RPC but gives no way for a new person to acquire it without an administrator knowing their user id. Scoped to link invites only: email invites need a transactional provider and deliverability handling for no additional capability in v1.

nodes.label: M5 — Work Item Model
nodes.rationale: The columns landed in M2-03 and the UI placeholders already existed and were inert — the design was ahead of the schema. Also where the card component's accumulated shortcuts get paid off.

nodes.label: M6 — Realtime
nodes.rationale: Written as one milestone doing two things; the 2026-08-14 revision keeps every task ID but stops treating them as one unit, because ordering and channels have different dependents and bundling them made the whole roadmap inherit the stricter of the two.

nodes.label: M6-A — Ordering by rank
nodes.rationale: Blocks any second surface that writes order. Built before M17 not for urgency but for cost: it rewrites useTodoDrop, reorderTodos, insertDense, applyTodoMoved and byPosition, and the redesign touches the same drag affordances.

nodes.label: M6-B — Realtime channels
nodes.rationale: Blocks nothing in the roadmap — it is a cache-update path, not a layout or a schema. Wants M6-A finished first, or every remote event re-applies a whole-column renumber from the sender's stale snapshot.

nodes.label: M7 — Comments & Activity
nodes.rationale: Split 2026-08-14: comments stay (after M6-B for live threads and M17 for where a thread renders), activity moves to M18 where it finally gets the reader M7-05 required before the table may exist.

nodes.label: M8 — Boards UX
nodes.rationale: Absorbed by M15, not cancelled: M8 assumed boards are a flat list belonging to a user, and every screen it describes changes shape when there is a level above it. Building them flat then adding spaces means building them twice. Its nine task bodies remain the specification.

nodes.label: M9 — Quality
nodes.rationale: Not polish — Accessible, Keyboard Friendly, Fast and Mobile Friendly are four stated core principles that do not currently hold. The real risk is perpetual deferral, at which point they quietly become aspirations.

nodes.label: M10 — Work Item Depth
nodes.rationale: Types, labels, subtasks and links: the largest single step toward Jira-level functional depth and the one with the most schema consequences. Epics-in-todos vs a second table must be decided before subtasks are built, not after.

nodes.label: M11 — Backlog & Views
nodes.rationale: The views half shipped early and M16 takes it over; the backlog half stays and is the one part that still hard-requires M6-A, because a backlog is a second ordered view and dense integers make two views renumber one column from two stale snapshots.

nodes.label: M12 — Search & Filtering
nodes.rationale: Filtering shipped exactly as specified — client-side over the existing cache, no migration, no dependency. Search moved to M16 because a view model without it would have to grow one later and every view would need retrofitting; saved filters and the command palette stay here.

nodes.label: M13 — Configurable Workflow
nodes.rationale: What separates a Kanban board from a work-management product, and deliberately last because it is the decision most expensive to get wrong early. Splitting statuses from columns is the only remaining migration that would touch every work item row, every policy and every DnD path at once.

nodes.label: M14 — Foundation Cleanup
nodes.rationale: First in build order because two of its decisions are one-way doors: the key prefix must be settled before a user can create a second board, and whether a space is a permission scope must be settled before any space exists. It blocks and is blocked by nothing.

nodes.label: M15 — Spaces & Boards
nodes.rationale: Establishes the hierarchy the redesign renders and the scope the view model needs a word for. Absorbs M8's nine task bodies; its cheapest starting point is services/boards/'s three mutation hooks that already exist with no UI consumer.

nodes.label: M16 — Shared View Model
nodes.rationale: Turns the shipped board pipeline into one four views share, so adding the fifth view is a renderer rather than a pipeline. Needed no schema at all, which is itself the finding: the pipeline was extendable without one.

nodes.label: M17 — Product Redesign
nodes.rationale: Renders a settled hierarchy (M15) over a settled view model (M16), and precedes Calendar and Timeline specifically so it can ship the view shell contract they slot into. A redesign that only redesigns the board would leave both new views to be re-hosted afterwards.

nodes.label: M18 — Activity & Overview
nodes.rationale: Activity and the Overview are one milestone because M7-05 forbade the log existing without a reader and the Overview's recent-activity panel is that reader. Building either alone ships a dead panel or an unbounded audit table.

nodes.label: M19 — Calendar
nodes.rationale: The cheap date view and the proof that M16's model survives a second axis — built before M20 pays for the same lesson with a migration. It forced four decisions rather than a task list, and discovered that due_date is timestamptz rather than the date this plan assumed.

nodes.label: M20 — Timeline
nodes.rationale: The only milestone in the 2026-08-14 direction that requires a schema change (todos.start_date), which is why the direction asked for it to be identified explicitly. No drag, deliberately: dragging a bar is two gestures wearing one affordance and neither is described in this plan.

nodes.label: Build order (not milestone number order)
nodes.rationale: Milestone numbers record the order milestones were written across three passes, not the order to build in. The build order is dependency-driven: every UI milestone runs after the hierarchy (M15) and the view model (M16), the two decisions that would otherwise force it to be rewritten.

nodes.label: GitHub Flow with milestone integration branches
nodes.rationale: The project is small, so heavyweight GitFlow costs more than it returns — with one exception: milestones performing destructive data migrations (M2, M3, M6) have intermediate states that are not deployable, so each gets a long-lived integration branch that merges to main once.

nodes.label: Expand → Backfill → Contract
nodes.rationale: Three phases, never one migration. Deploying the application code that reads the new shape between Backfill and Contract creates a window where both shapes are valid, so a bad deploy is a revert rather than an incident.

nodes.label: Forward-only migrations via the CLI
nodes.rationale: There is no supabase migration down, so rollback means a forward-fix migration — free, and therefore the backbone of this project's recovery story. Migrations live in Git and are applied only by the CLI: a schema change made in the dashboard is a schema change that does not exist.

nodes.label: Rule 6 — Tier A / Tier B migration classification
nodes.rationale: Recovery effort scales with what a migration can actually destroy. Tier A (policies, functions, triggers, constraints, new tables/columns) needs only the prior definition captured verbatim plus forward-fix SQL, and is never blocked on backup infrastructure. Tier B (DROP, type change, UPDATE/DELETE of existing rows) is where the money and the caution go.

nodes.label: Backup procedure (Tier B only)
nodes.rationale: A dump plus recorded row counts before any migration that can destroy data. Explicitly not a gate on Tier A — running it before a policy or function change proves nothing the migration's own verification block does not.

nodes.label: Task risk labels (SAFE / MEDIUM / HIGH RISK)
nodes.rationale: HIGH RISK does not mean 'needs backup infrastructure' — it means the change is easy to get wrong and expensive to notice. The mitigation is matched to the failure mode, which is why several HIGH RISK M3 tasks are Tier A and shipped without a dump, correctly.

nodes.label: Calibration — portfolio project sizing
nodes.rationale: The database holds fixtures, there are no users and no uptime commitment, so recovery machinery is sized to what a migration can destroy rather than to what a bank would do. What does not get relaxed is the security model: a portfolio project with a broken permission model is a worse portfolio project.

nodes.label: Definition of Done
nodes.rationale: build + lint + test green, every manual test box actually ticked, pure logic gets a test sibling, docs updated in the same PR. A milestone is done only when no task was silently dropped and no expand/backfill/contract sequence is left half-applied.

nodes.label: Code Review Checklist
nodes.rationale: Answer every line; do not skip lines that 'obviously' pass. Its permission section requires naming the policy, constraint, trigger or RPC that enforces any new rule server-side, and its realtime section requires cache-update logic to live in a pure function a channel handler can also call.

nodes.label: Testing Checklist
nodes.rationale: Smoke, multi-user roles, concurrency and regression, run in full after every milestone. Every negative expectation is proved with curl against PostgREST using that role's own JWT — the UI proves nothing about RLS, because it never asks for rows it does not expect.

nodes.label: Proof is REST-level, not UI-level
nodes.rationale: A hidden button is not a denied request. An INSERT denial raises 42501, but UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT denials are zero rows silently — so only row counts distinguish 'no policy at all' from 'a policy that permits everything'.

nodes.label: Permission Model (authoritative)
nodes.rationale: The single definition of who may do what; any task, policy, RPC or component that disagrees with it is wrong, including tasks written earlier in the document. It is a product requirement, explicitly not production hardening, and may never be moved to Part V.

nodes.label: Four roles — viewer → editor → admin → owner
nodes.rationale: Exactly four roles, each including everything the role to its left can do. No additional roles, and no replacing roles with ad-hoc boolean permission columns — a separate permission system is only justified if a requirement genuinely cannot be expressed as a role.

nodes.label: Board content matrix
nodes.rationale: Read for every role; create/update/delete/reorder of work items and columns for editor and above. Reordering is content, so a viewer cannot drag.

nodes.label: Membership matrix
nodes.rationale: Everyone sees the member list; admins manage viewers and editors; only the owner touches admins; nobody modifies the Owner. Leaving voluntarily is allowed for every role except the Owner.

nodes.label: Comment matrix
nodes.rationale: Decided M7-01: commenting is participation, not content, which is why a viewer appears here and not in the content matrix. A comment belongs to its author and the only power anyone else has is deletion — an admin who could edit someone's text would make the attribution a lie. Editing is narrowed to the text by a column-level grant update (content), because a row-level policy cannot say which columns an update may touch.

nodes.label: Strictly-below-own-rank rule
nodes.rationale: The role specification was genuinely ambiguous about whether an admin may act on another admin; resolved as no, because that is the reading that keeps promote/demote-admins as the Owner's distinguishing power. Changing it means changing this row, both matrices, M3-14's checks and M3-16's tests together.

nodes.label: Owner immutability invariants I1–I6
nodes.rationale: Database invariants, not UI rules: one Owner per board, whose membership row cannot be deleted or re-roled by any actor including themselves, and whose row an admin has no path to at all. I4 is stated separately from I2/I3 because a caller-rank check that stops at 'is the caller admin or owner' satisfies both and still lets an admin through. Changing who the Owner is is ownership transfer, not a membership operation.

nodes.label: Postgres is the authority; frontend checks are UX only
nodes.rationale: Rule 5 of the plan's non-negotiables: no task may introduce an authorization rule that exists only in React. The UI should tell the truth about permission — a viewer should not see affordances that will fail — but hiding a button is never the enforcement.

nodes.label: SECURITY DEFINER membership helpers
nodes.rationale: is_board_member, board_role and accessible_board_ids, all STABLE with an explicit empty search_path. board_role returns NULL for a non-member and NULL in (…) is NULL, which both USING and WITH CHECK treat as failure — non-membership is denied by the same expression that grades roles, with no separate branch to forget. accessible_board_ids was designed in M2-08 as the single swap point M3-05 widened to membership without editing one policy.

nodes.label: RLS recursion trap on board_members
nodes.rationale: A policy on board_members that itself queries board_members recurses infinitely and returns a hard 500. The remedy is the SECURITY DEFINER STABLE helpers, which must exist before any policy uses them.

nodes.label: board_members is never client-writable
nodes.rationale: Self-read policy only, with no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE policy, deliberately — every membership mutation goes through a SECURITY DEFINER RPC that performs its own check. M3-13 additionally revoked the table privileges, so Postgres refuses a direct write with 42501 before row security is even consulted: two independent mistakes deep.

nodes.label: board_roster RPC — explicit column exposure
nodes.rationale: RLS filters rows, not columns, and profiles carries email and bio — so a co-member SELECT policy would hand both over. A SECURITY DEFINER function is the only place the database can state which columns leave it, so the six-column return list (id, username, full_name, avatar_url, role, joined_at) is the exposure boundary and profiles stays self-only by design. A non-member gets a byte-identical empty result for a real and a fabricated board id, so the function is not an existence oracle.

nodes.label: Membership mutation RPCs (add / set_role / remove / leave)
nodes.rationale: Privilege-granting functions: the caller's role comes from board_role, never from an argument, and the 'target is never the Owner' check comes before the caller-rank gate deliberately, so it cannot be reached past an 'admin or owner' branch. The risk is a logic flaw, not data loss — no backup mitigates a function that lets an admin demote the Owner; only reading it does.

nodes.label: leave_board — consent as a separate operation
nodes.rationale: Built as its own function rather than a self-branch inside remove_board_member: a rule that reads 'remove_board_member happens to allow self' is one refactor away from disappearing, and the two operations have genuinely different authorization — one is administration, the other is consent. Membership you can be given and cannot decline is a defect, not a safeguard.

nodes.label: delete_column RPC (SECURITY INVOKER)
nodes.rationale: Rehome-then-delete is inherently multi-statement, so unlike the reorder RPC it does not go away with M6. Built SECURITY INVOKER so the caller's own RLS applies and it inherits the editor+ gate for free; the zero-row DELETE check raises 42501, turning a silent RLS denial into a real error — 'did the write actually happen' is the authorization check.

nodes.label: reorder_todos RPC (M3-10, closed as unnecessary)
nodes.rationale: Deferred rather than built because M6-04 would delete it, then closed in 2026-08-14: a move is now a single-row rank write, so no client-supplied array of ids and positions reaches the database on the drag path. The one surviving bulk renumber — M6-06's rebalance — takes an id and derives every value server-side, which is exactly the property this task asked for.

nodes.label: M3-16 role matrix acceptance verification
nodes.rationale: A separate task with its own commit because a verification folded into a feature task is a verification that gets skipped, and it gates the milestone. 105/105 on a replica, mutation-tested by reverting each rule to confirm the harness turns red; a re-run against the linked project is still owed. It exercises policies and table privileges but not the HTTP layer, which is named at the head of the file rather than papered over.

nodes.label: Composite FK — a work item's column must belong to its board
nodes.rationale: todos.board_id and todos.column_id were independent FKs, so an editor on board A could PATCH a work item with a column_id from board B and both USING and WITH CHECK would pass. One composite foreign key enforces it for every writer with no function to maintain — integrity, not authorization: it refuses the owner exactly as it refuses an editor. M7-01 repeats the shape one table further out for comments.

nodes.label: Boards own everything (ownership moves from user to board)
nodes.rationale: columns.user_id and todos.user_id were the ownership columns, and every remaining MVP feature is structurally impossible against them. Dropping user_id is the point of no return, which is why creator_id is backfilled first and why the drop is the last step of the contraction.

nodes.label: provision_new_user() RPC
nodes.rationale: The old client-side signup sequence was three separate writes with no transaction, so a failure mid-way left a half-provisioned account and nothing repaired it. One SECURITY DEFINER RPC, idempotent — it returns the caller's existing board, so a retried signup cannot mint a second one.

nodes.label: Per-board task key (board_key + BEFORE INSERT trigger)
nodes.rationale: Built as a trigger rather than the insert RPC the task suggested, and it is now the project's precedent for 'an invariant every writer must satisfy': an RPC only constrains callers who use it, a trigger constrains all of them. Keys are never reused. A consequence worth knowing: inserting a work item UPDATEs boards, which succeeds for a non-owner only because the trigger is SECURITY DEFINER.

nodes.label: boards.key_prefix
nodes.rationale: The trigger fires the day a user can create a second board, because both would hand out KAN-1 — and a key already in a URL, a comment or someone's notes is an identifier people rely on. The column default is the backfill (a Postgres 11+ fast default), so there is no data migration. A board moving between spaces must never renumber a card.

nodes.label: Client-minted UUID todo ids
nodes.rationale: Integer ids forced optimistic inserts to mint fake ids with Date.now(), colliding with the real sequence space and requiring an isOptimistic flag; they also leaked row counts. With client-generated UUIDs the optimistic row is the stored row, addTodo upserts, and realtime echo suppression becomes an identity match rather than bespoke de-duplication. Migrated in M2 precisely because no FKs pointed at todos.id yet.

nodes.label: Dense integer positions
nodes.rationale: Every reorder recomputes and bulk-upserts a whole column. With concurrent editors this is not a merge conflict but silent data loss, because each client renumbers from its own stale snapshot and last-write-wins across every row. Safe only while exactly one view can write order.

nodes.label: Fractional ranks (double precision)
nodes.rationale: The operation is 'a value strictly between these two', a float gives it in one step, and the failure mode is bounded and known — about 50 midpoints into one gap before the mantissa runs out, which rebalancing absorbs. rankBetween returns null before writing rather than discovering a collision afterwards. The backfill asserted inside its transaction that rank order equals position order on every column of every board.

nodes.label: Single-row rank writes on move
nodes.rationale: A move computes the midpoint between two neighbours and updates one row, replacing whole-column renumbering — which is what removed the reorder RPC's security case and what M6-B needs so a remote event does not re-apply a column renumber from the sender's snapshot.

nodes.label: Rank rebalancing RPCs
nodes.rationale: Repeated midpoint insertion exhausts precision, so the column is renumbered server-side. Built the way the reorder RPC required — takes an id and derives every new value in the database, so nothing about the resulting order comes from the client. It needs a Vitest test, not a manual check: nobody will reproduce precision exhaustion by hand.

nodes.label: board_id denormalised onto every board-scoped child table
nodes.rationale: The membership helpers take a board id; without a denormalised board_id every policy evaluation joins the child table back to todos on every row. It is a derived key used by the security boundary, not duplicated user data — the one documented exception to 'never store duplicated information'. Decided once at M7-01 so attachments, labels and activities do not each invent a different design.

nodes.label: comments table
nodes.rationale: Carries board_id for the policy predicate and a composite FK to (todos.id, board_id) so a comment's board cannot drift from its work item's. Written and verified against a shadow database at 32/32; not yet pushed to the linked project. Comments are loaded per open work item, never joined into the board fetch.

nodes.label: activities table (trigger-written)
nodes.rationale: Conditional on a reader existing — an unbounded audit table with no reader grows forever and is silently wrong the day the UI is built. No client write policy at all: triggers are the only writer, which is what makes the log trustworthy. Record the actor rather than inferring it at read time, and a row must still explain itself after the row it points at is deleted. Membership changes are the entries most worth having and the ones a client-written log would never capture honestly.

nodes.label: board_invites and the invite RPCs
nodes.rationale: An invite that bypasses the membership matrix is a second, weaker permission system, so role is constrained to admin/editor/viewer at the column level and an admin may not create an admin invite. Acceptance is atomic and idempotent — accepting twice is a clean no-op and accepting while already a member changes nothing in either direction, which is what makes a leaked old link harmless.

nodes.label: todos.start_date
nodes.rationale: Two dates rather than a duration (which makes the end derived and recomputed by every reader) or a schedule child table (a second set of policies, cache functions and handlers to hold two dates). Shipped timestamptz, not date, because due_date always was one — and a mixed-type CHECK is not IMMUTABLE, so the range constraint could not have been created at all.

nodes.label: Drop todos.status / previous_status
nodes.rationale: Two dead columns that look like status, with M10 adding type and M13 adding a real status concept — three status-shaped things in one table is a trap for whoever reads the schema next. Tier B, so blocked on the backup procedure; the migration was deliberately not written, because db push applies every pending file and a parked file would be swept in without its dump.

nodes.label: Avatar storage path hole
nodes.rationale: Found by the M0-06 audit and unowned for weeks: any authenticated user could upsert over another person's avatar because the path was a guessable <uid>.<ext>. A live authorization bug, explicitly not production hardening. Closed in M14 by scoping storage writes to the caller's own folder; SELECT stays public because avatars are public by product design. Its shape is the template for M10's attachments.

nodes.label: A space is filing, not a permission scope
nodes.rationale: The alternative is a space role and a board role that can disagree, a precedence rule between them, a second set of RPCs and a second matrix — a whole second authorization system bought for filing. Spaces are owner-only; a member who does not own the space sees the board unfiled. Reversible without a rewrite: if spaces later need sharing, spaces gains membership and boards.space_id is unchanged.

nodes.label: Board filing rule (only the owner files, and only into a space they own)
nodes.rationale: The spec's rule ('only into a space the caller owns') was necessary and not sufficient: space_id is one column on a shared row, so an admin could file a colleague's board into their own space and it would silently leave the owner's sidebar. Implemented as a BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE trigger, not a WITH CHECK, because a policy sees only the new row and could not tell whether space_id changed — and a conjunct would have refused an admin renaming a filed board.

nodes.label: AuthProvider — one subscription per page load
nodes.rationale: useAuth was a plain hook, so four call sites each opened their own getSession and onAuthStateChange and flipped their own loading. Hoisting it also gives one place to clear the query cache on SIGNED_OUT — however the session ends, not only via the logout button.

nodes.label: Query key factory
nodes.rationale: Keys were inline string literals across a dozen files, which blocks per-board caching and hides mismatches — a mistyped key means a mutation writes to a cache nothing reads, which looks like 'the UI didn't update'. No key is spelled out anywhere else.

nodes.label: Board-scoped query keys
nodes.rationale: boardId is a required argument even where it may be undefined, so 'find every place that reads the board' is a compiler error rather than a grep. One flat array per board, not per column. A persisted cache with a global todos key is exactly where cross-user leakage happens, which is why persistence stayed unwired until keys were scoped.

nodes.label: Pure cache-update functions
nodes.rationale: The single cheapest thing M2 could do for M6: a channel handler cannot reach into an onMutate closure, so the transformations live outside as pure (rows, …) => rows functions that mutations and realtime handlers both call. None mutates its input — onMutate snapshots the cached array for rollback and the cache holds those very objects, so renumbering in place would leave onError nothing to restore.

nodes.label: Optimistic write with snapshot rollback
nodes.rationale: onMutate cancels queries and snapshots, onError restores, and the failure is visible to the user rather than only to the cache. A mutation with an optimistic write and no rollback does not merge — the old drop path left the UI permanently inconsistent with the database, silently, until the next refetch.

nodes.label: Global mutation error surfacing
nodes.rationale: Not one mutation had a user-visible onError, so a silently-failing RLS policy looked identical to success — this is what makes every later milestone observable. The MutationCache toasts rejected mutations and the QueryCache toasts only failed refetches, since a failed first load is already rendered by the component that owns the query. Expect previously-invisible failures to start appearing; that is the feature.

nodes.label: Error boundaries and route errorElements
nodes.rationale: A render throw in any card blanked the whole application. Each column's card list is wrapped so one bad card costs that list and nothing else, with route errorElements as the outer net — render throws are a separate failure path from mutation errors.

nodes.label: Vitest as the only test mechanism
nodes.rationale: Pulled forward from M9 because nine milestones of schema migrations and realtime races cannot be defended by two self-check files. The *.check.ts scripts were ported and deleted so there is one way to run tests, not two. No React Testing Library yet — pure logic is where the risk is, and component tests nobody needs are a maintenance tax.

nodes.label: Shared view pipeline (scope → filter → search → sort → group → render)
nodes.rationale: One model that Board, List, Calendar and Timeline are four renderings of, so the fifth view is a renderer rather than a pipeline. Grouping deliberately stays at the view: it is the same groupTodos, but a swimlane and a section header need it at different points in their markup. A view that cannot express itself over this pipeline is a finding about the pipeline, not a licence to fork it.

nodes.label: View registry with capabilities
nodes.rationale: A view as a value — key, label, and canReorder/canGroup/canSort — so dndDisabled is derived rather than hand-coded per view, and 'does this view write order?' has an answer instead of a code review. Its test asserts exactly one view can reorder, which is the earliest possible warning that dense integers are no longer safe.

nodes.label: ViewScope (board | space | all)
nodes.rationale: A view needs a scope, and 'space' does not exist until M15. The shipped board pipeline was board-scoped by construction, which is precisely why the Overview's cross-board reach had to be designed rather than discovered.

nodes.label: Cross-board data: per-board queries unioned client-side
nodes.rationale: Option (a) over a scope-keyed query: the decisive argument is not request count but that a second cache shape holding the same rows twice forks the write path M2-16 unified and M6-B depends on. Because ['todos', boardId] kept its exact meaning, not one mutation had to be touched.

nodes.label: Client-side filtering over the cached board array
nodes.rationale: Nearly free and correct up to the board size the cache holds; server-side filtering is a new query shape, a new cache key per filter and a new interaction with the PostgREST max_rows cap. Move server-side when a board outgrows the cache and record the threshold then — the same trigger as the cursor-pagination deferral.

nodes.label: Panels are search params, not routes
nodes.rationale: ?task=<id> keeps the board mounted behind the panel, carries the view state along in the same URL, and makes Back close it — so one link carries the task and the view it was found under. Every drawer M17 adds follows the same contract; a drawer that is a route is a second answer to a question already answered.

nodes.label: Task Detail surface — three regions decided once
nodes.rationale: Five milestones each want to add something to the panel, and the failure mode is each appending a section and the panel being rewritten four times. Header, a fields list where every new property is a row, and a tabbed lower region created by the first capability that needs it. No column or table is added because the panel has a space for it — a tab with nothing behind it is the placeholder M17 spent a pass deleting.

nodes.label: View shell contract
nodes.rationale: Identity slot, toolbar slot, content area and drawer, defined once, so Calendar and Timeline add a registry entry and a renderer and no layout. This is why the redesign precedes the two new views rather than following them.

nodes.label: Hand-rolled drag and drop
nodes.rationale: A differentiator, not a checkbox: the custom collision detection picks the gap nearest the pointer rather than by rect intersection, and library defaults were not good enough. The redesign is explicitly forbidden from changing the interaction model, and keyboard support is not a config flag because collisionDetection reads pointerCoordinates first — it needs a parallel index-based path.

nodes.label: Calendar drop resolution (closestCenter over day cells)
nodes.rationale: The board answers 'which gap between which two cards'; a calendar answers 'which day' over big rectangles with no internal order, so it is a different strategy and touches none of the board's. A drop writes due_date through the existing update mutation — views do not get their own write paths, and a second optimistic layer is ruled out.

nodes.label: No timezone conversion in the calendar
nodes.rationale: All date maths is string maths over YYYY-MM-DD, with Date appearing only inside two helpers via Date.UTC and always discarded. This is what makes a task due the 14th appear on the 14th for everyone — and the rule became more load-bearing, not less, once due_date turned out to be timestamptz rather than the date the plan assumed.

nodes.label: Timeline row order is derived, never stored
nodes.rationale: A Gantt whose rows can be dragged into an arbitrary order is a second ranked surface, which would reopen the reorder RPC and pull M6-A forward the day it ships. Deriving order from start_date costs nothing and keeps todos.position at exactly one writer; the registry test guards it.

nodes.label: React Compiler removed (M9-04 decision)
nodes.rationale: Measured on this codebase: 2.7x build time and +25% on the board chunk, against auto-memoisation nobody has profiled. The reason is the asymmetry, not the numbers — enabling a blanket memoiser before M9-05's profiling contradicts that task's own instruction to memoise only what the profiler names. The ambiguity (plugin commented out, README claiming it was on) was the real defect.

nodes.label: Jira as functional reference, not UI reference
nodes.rationale: A feature is in scope if it adds capability; it is out of scope if its only justification is that Jira's screen looks like that. The work item model, roles, workflows, filters and history are borrowed; the interaction model, keyboard model and visual identity are ours.

nodes.label: UX principle — board context is never lost
nodes.rationale: Inspecting or editing a work item should not feel like navigating away from the board — the single strongest argument against a full-page issue view as the primary interaction.

nodes.label: UX principle — one data model, many views
nodes.rationale: Board, backlog and list are views over the same work items, not separate features with separate state. Any schema decision that makes a second view expensive is a bad schema decision.

nodes.label: Terminology — 'work item' is the product word, todos is the table
nodes.rationale: Renaming the table would touch every policy, index, FK, cache function, realtime publication and query key for zero user-visible gain. The rename is explicitly rejected, not deferred.

nodes.label: Part V — Deferred / Production Hardening
nodes.rationale: Real concerns kept and costed rather than deleted, each with the trigger that reopens it — mostly 'the project takes real users'. The permission model, owner immutability, the no-client-write rule on board_members, the role verification and the avatar hole may never be moved here: deferring recovery tooling is a budget decision, deferring authorization would be a defect.

nodes.label: PH-01 — PITR deferred
nodes.rationale: ~$125/month uncapped to insure two accounts and 21 work items; its window starts at enablement so it protects nothing already stored, and a PITR restore is a whole-project rollback — the wrong instrument for reverting a policy. It once blocked the entire permission model, which was the wrong trade. Reopens before the next Tier B migration or when real user data exists.

nodes.label: PH-03 — RLS membership performance verification
nodes.rationale: Seeding 500 cards to measure a fixture-scale app measures a problem that does not exist; the structural mitigation (both board_members indexes) is already in place. Re-anchored 2026-08-14 to a concrete trigger: before M18's cross-board query ships, because it is the first query whose cost is proportional to everything the caller can see rather than to one board.

nodes.label: Appendix B — Deferred Decisions
nodes.rationale: A deferral is a decision, not an omission — if one is skipped without a note it becomes invisible debt. Every row carries the trigger that reopens it, and rows are struck through rather than deleted when the trigger fires.

nodes.label: Appendix D — Forward Schema Decisions
nodes.rationale: Only decisions whose delay makes the eventual change structurally harder — a migration touching every row or policy, or an FK other tables have started pointing at. A nullable column that can be added cheaply at any time is deliberately not on the list, because adding it early would be speculative work.

nodes.label: Appendix E — Explicitly Out of Scope
nodes.rationale: Listing refusals is the point: an unlisted feature gets re-argued every few months, and 'Jira has it' is not a requirement. Two questions decide the list — does it add capability or resemblance, and does the thing it depends on already exist and get used.

nodes.label: Board ownership transfer (deferred)
nodes.rationale: Invariant I6 scopes it out: changing who the Owner is is not a membership operation, and until a separate explicitly-scoped operation exists the Owner of a board never changes. It must not be smuggled into a membership RPC or a boards UPDATE.

Shared view architecture (M16 + M17 contracts the later views fill)
